prompt:
# Subject Merge Area Partition

## Quick Start

Create broad topic areas for one subject so later calls compare nearby candidates instead of the whole inventory. Use only the provided candidate cards.

## Decision Rules

- Partition by teachable neighborhood, not by exact duplicate identity.
- Prefer small, coherent neighborhoods over one large catch-all area.
- A full subject should usually have 15-25 areas when enough candidates exist.
- Put every input candidate ID in exactly one area.
- Keep mixed-language versions of the same topic in the same area.
- Do not decide final merges here. This step only creates neighborhoods.

## Output

Return one JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "area_001",
      "label": "Short topic area",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates belong in the same broad neighborhood.",
      "candidate_ids": ["candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-Check

- Every input candidate ID appears exactly once.
- No area is a miscellaneous dump unless the input truly has isolated topics.
- Area labels describe topics, not final accepted concepts.
- No web search or external knowledge was used.

candidates.label: Linear Thinking and Exponential Change
candidates.description: The cognitive limitation that humans think linearly, making it difficult to properly assess exponential technological growth, which can lead to flawed decisions about technology adoption.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-making process and fundamentals of decision-making approaches.

candidates.label: Outcome Bias and Evaluating Decision Quality
candidates.description: Outcome bias is the tendency to evaluate the quality of a decision based solely on its outcomes.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-making process and fundamentals of decision-making approaches.

candidates.label: Problem Framing Definition and Importance
candidates.description: Problem framing is the process of discovering and defining the real problem before seeking solutions.

candidates.label: Cognitive Biases that Lead to Premature Convergence
candidates.description: Premature convergence is the tendency to jump to solutions quickly, driven by pattern completion and confirmation bias.

candidates.label: Organizational Pressures that Reinforce Solution-Jumping
candidates.description: Organizational systems such as business case templates, status meetings, and budgeting processes can inadvertently push teams toward quick solutions before adequate problem framing, reinforcing premature convergence at an institutional level.

candidates.label: Double Diamond Model for Problem Framing
candidates.description: The Double Diamond model is a framework for problem framing consisting of two phases: Discover (divergent thinking to explore the problem space) and Define (convergent thinking to crystallize the problem).

candidates.label: Problem Reframing Technique
candidates.description: Problem reframing is the deliberate restating of a strategic question to expose new perspectives, risks, and opportunities.

candidates.label: Impact of Poor Framing on AI Effectiveness
candidates.description: AI systems optimize for the problem they are given.

candidates.label: Strategies for Building a Problem Framing Culture
candidates.description: Leaders can embed problem framing into organizational culture by shifting focus from 'how to fix' to 'why this happens', and by establishing habits such as asking reflective questions, standardizing problem statements, and adding diagnostic phases before solutioning.

candidates.label: Benefits of Problem Framing for Execution Clarity
candidates.description: A well-framed problem clarifies ownership, metrics, and cross-functional involvement, leading to more efficient execution with fewer mid-course corrections.

candidates.label: Applying Problem Framing to Thought Leadership
candidates.description: In thought leadership, starting with a clearly defined problem rather than a broad audience attracts the right followers.

candidates.label: Description Invariance
candidates.description: A normative principle of classical decision theory stating that rational agents' choices should not depend on the particular way options are described, as long as the descriptions are logically equivalent.

candidates.label: Framing Effects and Preference Reversals
candidates.description: Framing effects occur when different but logically equivalent descriptions of a decision problem lead to systematic preference reversals, violating description invariance.

candidates.label: Prospect Theory as Explanation for Framing Effects
candidates.description: Prospect theory explains framing effects via a reference-dependent value function, loss aversion, and the principle that people are risk-averse for gains and risk-seeking for losses.

candidates.label: Adaptiveness of Decision Processes in Framing
candidates.description: Framing effects are not purely irrational; they reflect adaptive mechanisms in human judgment and choice, which may serve important functions in real-world decision-making.

candidates.label: Payoff Table Structure
candidates.description: A payoff table organizes decision alternatives (rows) and states of nature (columns), with payoffs in cells representing outcomes.

candidates.label: Maximax (Optimistic) Criterion
candidates.description: An optimistic approach: select the alternative with the best possible outcome.

candidates.label: Maximin (Conservative) Criterion
candidates.description: A conservative approach: select the alternative with the best worst-case outcome.

candidates.label: Minimax Regret Criterion
candidates.description: A decision criterion that minimizes the maximum regret.

candidates.label: Laplace Criterion
candidates.description: A decision criterion that assumes all states of nature are equally likely and selects the alternative with the highest average payoff.

candidates.label: Hurwicz Criterion
candidates.description: A decision criterion that balances optimism and pessimism using a coefficient of optimism (α).

candidates.label: Laplace Criterion (Equally Likely/Insufficient Reason)
candidates.description: Decision rule that assumes all states of nature are equally likely, computing the average payoff for each alternative and selecting the highest average.

candidates.label: Hurwicz Criterion (Weighted Optimism/Pessimism)
candidates.description: Decision rule that balances best and worst payoffs using a coefficient of optimism α, computing weighted average: α*best + (1-α)*worst, and selects the highest.

candidates.label: Decision Environments
candidates.description: Four types of decision contexts: certainty (known outcomes), uncertainty (no probability information), risk (known probabilities), and conflict (adversarial decisions).

candidates.label: Payoff Table as a Decision Tool
candidates.description: A table that organizes payoffs for each decision alternative under various states of nature, used as input to decision criteria.

candidates.label: Maximax Criterion (Optimistic)
candidates.description: Optimistic rule: choose the alternative with the maximum possible payoff (best of the best).

candidates.label: Maximin Criterion (Pessimistic)
candidates.description: Pessimistic rule: choose the alternative with the best worst-case payoff (guarantee a minimum).

candidates.label: Minimax Regret Criterion
candidates.description: Minimize maximum regret: construct regret table, find worst regret for each alternative, choose the smallest worst regret.

candidates.label: Expected Value Criterion (Decision under Risk)
candidates.description: When probabilities are known, compute expected monetary value for each alternative and choose the highest.

candidates.label: Decision Tree Definition and Purpose
candidates.description: A decision tree is a graphical model used for decision-making under uncertainty.

candidates.label: Decision Tree Symbols and Conventions
candidates.description: Decision trees use standardized symbols: squares for decision nodes, circles for chance (probability) nodes, and triangles for end (outcome) nodes.

candidates.label: Constructing a Decision Tree
candidates.description: To build a decision tree, begin with a square decision node, draw branches for each alternative, attach circles for chance events where outcomes are uncertain, draw branches for each possible outcome, and end with payoffs.

candidates.label: Labeling Branches with Probabilities and Payoffs
candidates.description: On a decision tree, each branch from a chance node is labeled with the probability of that outcome and the associated monetary payoff.

candidates.label: Calculating Expected Value (EMV) at Chance Nodes
candidates.description: The expected value at a chance node is computed by multiplying each outcome's payoff by its probability and summing these products.

candidates.label: Folding Back to Determine the Optimal Decision
candidates.description: Folding back solves a decision tree from right to left: at each chance node, compute the EMV; at each decision node, select the alternative with the highest EMV and discard others.

candidates.label: Expected Monetary Value (EMV) Criterion
candidates.description: The EMV criterion selects the decision alternative with the highest expected monetary value, calculated as the probability-weighted average of all possible monetary outcomes.

candidates.label: Sensitivity Analysis in Decision Models
candidates.description: Sensitivity analysis examines how changes in input parameters (e.g., probabilities, payoffs) affect the optimal decision and EMV.

candidates.label: Bayes' Rule for Updating Probabilities
candidates.description: Bayes' rule computes posterior probabilities given prior probabilities and new evidence: P(B_i|A) = [P(A|B_i) P(B_i)] / Σ[P(A|B_j) P(B_j)].

candidates.label: Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI)
candidates.description: EVSI is the difference between the EMV with free sample information and the EMV without that information.

candidates.label: Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI)
candidates.description: EVPI is the difference between the EMV with free perfect information and the EMV without information.

candidates.label: Multistage Decision Problems and Contingency Plans
candidates.description: Multistage decisions involve alternating decisions and uncertain outcomes over time.

candidates.label: Utility Functions and Risk Aversion
candidates.description: A utility function U(x) transforms monetary values into utilities to capture risk attitudes.

candidates.label: Exponential Utility Function and Risk Tolerance
candidates.description: An exponential utility function has the form U(x) = 1 - e^{-x/R}, where R is the risk tolerance parameter.

candidates.label: Certainty Equivalent
candidates.description: The certainty equivalent of a risky prospect is the guaranteed monetary amount that makes a decision maker indifferent between the certain amount and the uncertain prospect.

candidates.label: Net Benefit Calculation at Decision Nodes
candidates.description: At a decision node, the cost of each option is subtracted from its expected outcome value to compute net benefit.

candidates.label: Sunk Costs in Decision Making
candidates.description: Sunk costs are past expenditures that cannot be recovered and should not influence current decisions.

candidates.label: Importance of Reliable Inputs in Decision Tree Analysis
candidates.description: The validity of a decision tree depends on a comprehensive list of probable outcomes and accurate estimates of probabilities and values.

candidates.label: Risk Profiles
candidates.description: A risk profile lists all possible monetary outcomes of a decision along with their probabilities, often visualized as a bar chart.

candidates.label: Handling Deterministic Payoffs in Decision Trees
candidates.description: When an alternative yields a single certain payoff regardless of the states of nature, it can be represented as a single branch without a chance node, simplifying the decision tree structure.

candidates.label: Definition and everyday examples of heuristics
candidates.description: Heuristics are mental shortcuts or rules of thumb developed from past experiences that enable quick decisions, sacrificing optimality for speed.

candidates.label: Limitations and intellectual humility regarding heuristics
candidates.description: Heuristics can lead to over-reliance in areas like political views, causing uninformed positions and resistance to facts.

candidates.label: Monte Carlo Simulation Definition and Process
candidates.description: A method that assigns probability distributions to uncertain inputs, uses random sampling to simulate thousands of outcomes, and analyzes the statistical results.

candidates.label: Business Value and Communication of Monte Carlo Simulation
candidates.description: Monte Carlo simulation helps CFOs replace opinion-based forecasting with data-driven odds, quantify risks, and communicate more confidently to stakeholders.

candidates.label: Financial Distributions for Monte Carlo: Normal, Triangular, Uniform
candidates.description: For Monte Carlo simulation in financial forecasting, three useful distributions are normal (mean and standard deviation), triangular (minimum, most likely, maximum) often mapping to bear/base/bull cases, and uniform (equal likelihood within a range).

candidates.label: Interpreting Simulation Output with Percentiles
candidates.description: Monte Carlo simulations produce a probability distribution of outcomes; percentiles (e.g., 10th, 50th, 90th) quantify the range of possible outcomes.

candidates.label: Multi-Input Monte Carlo Forecasting
candidates.description: Monte Carlo can handle complex equations with multiple uncertain inputs (e.g., regional revenues and expense categories).

candidates.label: Estimating Standard Deviation from Range (Range/4 Rule)
candidates.description: When using a normal distribution without a known standard deviation, a quick estimate is to divide the range (max - min) by 4.

candidates.label: The Problem with Single-Number Forecasts: Certainty Trap and Deterministic Models
candidates.description: Deterministic models produce a single outcome based on fixed inputs, creating an illusion of certainty (the certainty trap).

candidates.label: Risk vs. Uncertainty
candidates.description: Risk involves situations where probabilities can be calculated from known outcomes (e.g., roulette), while uncertainty involves unknown probabilities requiring judgment (e.g., launching new technology).

candidates.label: Comparing Risk Profiles for Decision Making
candidates.description: Even when projects have the same expected value, Monte Carlo can reveal different risk profiles.

candidates.label: Limitations: Simulation Organises Ignorance
candidates.description: Monte Carlo simulation does not eliminate uncertainty or predict the future; it structures our understanding of ignorance by mapping possible outcomes.

candidates.label: Excel Implementation of Monte Carlo Simulation
candidates.description: To implement Monte Carlo in Excel: model uncertain inputs (e.g., Sales, Costs) with mean and standard deviation; generate random trials using =NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, std_dev) for each input; run thousands of trials efficiently with a Data Table that recalculates a linked profit f

candidates.label: Analyzing Simulation Output in Excel
candidates.description: After running a Monte Carlo simulation in Excel, analyze the results by calculating descriptive statistics (AVERAGE, MIN, MAX) to understand central tendency and range, and use COUNTIFS to count outcomes below a threshold (e.g., profit < 0) to quantify risk as a percentage.

candidates.label: Sensitivity Analysis by Changing Input Parameters
candidates.description: After building the simulation, change an input mean (e.g., Fixed Costs) to observe the impact on risk of loss, demonstrating how Monte Carlo simulation supports decision-making under uncertainty.

candidates.label: Explicit Decision-Making Procedure
candidates.description: Groups should spell out the decision-making process ahead of time; following an explicit procedure leads to more effective decisions.

candidates.label: Strategies for Effective Group Discussion
candidates.description: Practical techniques to improve group decision-making, including encouraging all members to participate and thoroughly discussing the advantages and disadvantages of each option before deciding.

candidates.label: Three types of organizational decisions
candidates.description: Organizations face big-bet, cross-cutting, and delegated decisions, each requiring different approaches for success.

candidates.label: Widespread ineffectiveness of decision-making time
candidates.description: A majority of respondents spend over 30% of their time on decisions, but 61% say most of that time is used ineffectively, leading to large hidden costs for organizations.

candidates.label: Speed and quality are not trade-offs
candidates.description: Faster organizational decisions tend to be higher in quality; companies do not need to sacrifice quality for speed.

candidates.label: Foundational practice: decide at the right level
candidates.description: Winning organizations delegate decisions to the appropriate level, often with fewer reporting layers, which increases speed and quality.

candidates.label: Foundational practice: focus on enterprise-level value
candidates.description: Winning organizations align decisions with corporate strategy and allocate resources to high-value projects.

candidates.label: Foundational practice: get commitment from stakeholders
candidates.description: Winning organizations build commitment to executing decisions by involving accountable stakeholders and ensuring a robust process.

candidates.label: Big-bet best practice: quality of debate
candidates.description: For big-bet decisions, winning organizations ensure high-quality debate by exploring alternatives, seeking disconfirming information, and using a devil’s advocate.

candidates.label: Cross-cutting best practice: meeting process and coordination
candidates.description: For cross-cutting decisions, winning organizations emphasize effective coordination among stakeholders and focus meeting time on the most critical issues.

candidates.label: Delegated decisions best practice: empowerment
candidates.description: For delegated decisions, winning organizations empower employees through coaching and providing space for safe failure, fostering ownership and a bias for action.

candidates.label: The Tyranny of Metrics
candidates.description: A pitfall where quantitative targets and KPIs distort behavior, leading to unintended negative consequences that undermine the original goals.

candidates.label: Misinterpreting Correlations as Causation
candidates.description: The error of assuming that a statistical correlation between two variables implies a cause-and-effect relationship, without considering confounding factors.

candidates.label: Overgeneralizing from Limited Data Sets
candidates.description: The risk of drawing broad conclusions from internal data sets that may not represent the full picture, leading to poor decisions when the data is extrapolated beyond its actual scope.

candidates.label: Filter Bubbles and Confirmation Bias in Data Teams
candidates.description: The tendency for data teams to only seek information that confirms their existing beliefs, creating an echo chamber that overlooks contradictory insights and black swan events.

candidates.label: Losing the Human Element in Data-Driven Decisions
candidates.description: The pitfall of overemphasizing quantitative data to the point where important human factors—such as skills, relationships, and cultural fit—are overlooked.

candidates.label: Definition and Properties of Intuition in Strategic Decision-Making
candidates.description: Intuition is rapid, automatic, unconscious, and affectively charged, synthesizing experience and information to provide a holistic 'gut feeling' that guides decisions.

candidates.label: CEO Core Self-Evaluations as a Trigger for Intuition Use
candidates.description: Executives with high core self-evaluations (self-esteem, self-efficacy, internal locus of control) are more confident relying on intuition.

candidates.label: Cognitive Style and Cognitive Diversity in Intuitive Decision-Making
candidates.description: The CEO's cognitive style (preference for intuition vs.

candidates.label: Expertise as a Driver and Moderator of Intuition's Reliability
candidates.description: Expertise, built through extensive experience and deliberate practice, enables accurate intuitive pattern recognition.

candidates.label: Decision Framing and Familiarity as Intuition Triggers
candidates.description: Decisions framed as threats may trigger intuitive or analytical responses depending on firm size.

candidates.label: Firm-Level Factors Influencing Intuition Use
candidates.description: Smaller firms allow more intuitive decision-making due to agility.

candidates.label: Team Power Structure and Psychological Safety as Moderators of Intuition
candidates.description: Centralized power enables one person's intuition to drive decisions but risks unbridled intuition.

candidates.label: Contextual Enhancers of Intuition Effectiveness
candidates.description: Intuition is more effective under time pressure, high uncertainty, in M&A decisions (soft issues), and in dynamic or services industries where information is incomplete or change is rapid.

candidates.label: Causes of Intuitive Misses in Strategic Decisions
candidates.description: Intuition fails when there is excessive reliance without rational checking, dominant actor power centralization, lack of integration of diverse intuitions, or when applied to unfamiliar domains.

candidates.label: Rational Decision-Making: Success and Failure Conditions
candidates.description: Rational processes excel in stable or hostile environments and when firms have resources for analysis.

candidates.label: Practical Implications for Improving Intuitive Decision-Making
candidates.description: Organizations should develop intuitive awareness in education, encourage executives to embrace intuition mindfully, and foster expertise through deliberate practice and feedback.

candidates.label: Real options definition and contrast with DCF/NPV
candidates.description: Real options extend financial options theory to business investments, capturing the value of flexibility and learning under uncertainty that traditional DCF/NPV undervalues.

candidates.label: Learning and adaptive behavior in real options
candidates.description: Real option value stems from the ability to observe outcomes (learn) and adjust actions (adaptive behavior).

candidates.label: Using payoff diagrams to identify real options
candidates.description: A real option exists when the payoff structure resembles a call or put option diagram, featuring a kinked payoff limiting downside losses while allowing upside gains.

candidates.label: Three definitional characteristics of a real option
candidates.description: To qualify as a real option, an asset or decision must have: (1) a clearly defined underlying asset whose value varies unpredictably, (2) contingent payoffs triggered by a specific event, and (3) a limited life.

candidates.label: Exclusivity as driver of significant option value
candidates.description: An option has significant economic value only if the holder has exclusivity—the sole right to exercise it.

candidates.label: Six determinants of real option value
candidates.description: The value of a real option is driven by six factors: underlying asset value, variance of that value, expected dividends, strike price, option life, and risk-free interest rate.

candidates.label: Replication and arbitrage principles in option pricing
candidates.description: Option pricing models rely on: (1) replication—constructing a portfolio of the underlying asset and borrowing/lending that mimics the option's payoffs; (2) arbitrage—if two assets have identical payoffs, they must have the same price.

candidates.label: Model choice: Black-Scholes vs. binomial for real options
candidates.description: The Black-Scholes model assumes European exercise, constant variance, and no jumps, requiring only six inputs.

candidates.label: Three tests for applying real option valuation
candidates.description: To validly apply real option valuation, three tests must be passed: (1) identify an embedded option, (2) verify exclusivity, (3) ensure the underlying asset and option are tradeable enough for option pricing models to work.

candidates.label: Proactive vs. reactive flexibility in real options
candidates.description: Reactive flexibility involves optimally exercising an existing option; proactive flexibility means managers can influence option value levers (e.g., increase uncertainty, extend duration) before exercise.

candidates.label: Strategic lever selection via sensitivity analysis
candidates.description: Managers can decide which real option levers to influence by performing sensitivity analysis, revealing that increasing revenues (stock price) and cutting costs (exercise price) often have the largest impact on option value.

candidates.label: Excel Data Model basics
candidates.description: The Excel Data Model is a feature that lets you combine multiple tables into a single pivot table by creating relationships.
candidates.lesson_title: Excel Data Modeling and Analysis for Business

candidates.label: Creating relationships in the Excel Data Model
candidates.description: Excel can automatically detect relationships between tables based on matching field names or values, or users can manually create them via the Relationships dialog.
candidates.lesson_title: Excel Data Modeling and Analysis for Business

candidates.label: Monte Carlo Simulation for Risk Assessment
candidates.description: Stochastic modeling uses probability distributions to simulate risk factors, generating a full distribution of outcomes rather than a single point estimate, enabling more informed decision-making.
candidates.lesson_title: From Model Outputs to Business Recommendations

candidates.label: Sensitivity Analysis to Identify Key Risk Factors
candidates.description: Sensitivity analysis uses tornado graphs and spider charts to rank risk factors by their impact on the output criterion, helping prioritize factors for risk management.
candidates.lesson_title: From Model Outputs to Business Recommendations

candidates.label: Risk Mapping for Preliminary Risk Identification
candidates.description: Risk mapping uses expert assessment to score probability and impact, creating a matrix that categorizes risks to guide quantitative analysis.
candidates.lesson_title: From Model Outputs to Business Recommendations

candidates.label: Project Comparison Using Simulation Statistics
candidates.description: When comparing projects using simulation results, apply decision rules based on mean, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and skewness to select the best project.
candidates.lesson_title: From Model Outputs to Business Recommendations

candidates.label: Cognitive Biases that Distort Risk Decisions
candidates.description: Decision makers often rely on cognitive simplifications that lead to biases such as prior hypothesis, adjustment/anchoring, escalating commitment, and insensitivity to predictability, which can cause errors in risk assessment.
candidates.lesson_title: Defending Decisions Under Uncertainty: handling questions and stakeholder pushback

candidates.label: Risk as both a threat and an opportunity
candidates.description: When defending a decision under uncertainty, it is effective to acknowledge that risk includes both negative dangers and positive opportunities.
candidates.lesson_title: Defending Decisions Under Uncertainty: handling questions and stakeholder pushback

candidates.label: Scenario planning for stress-testing assumptions and preparing responses
candidates.description: Scenario planning simulates plausible risk events to help leaders stress-test strategic assumptions and practice responses.
candidates.lesson_title: Defending Decisions Under Uncertainty: handling questions and stakeholder pushback

candidates.label: Strategic Discipline for AI-Augmented Decision-Making
candidates.description: Before integrating AI into decisions, organizations should treat decision-making as a strategic discipline and intentionally design human-machine relationships.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-Making in the Age of AI

candidates.label: Preserving Human Agency in AI Decisions
candidates.description: Maintain human agency by building accountability, ensuring decision-makers understand (not just comply with) AI outputs, and clearly connecting choices to choosers.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-Making in the Age of AI

candidates.label: Human Purpose and Judgment as Irreplaceable by AI
candidates.description: Technology can speed up analysis and reduce uncertainty, but it cannot substitute human purpose, values, and judgment behind choices.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-Making in the Age of AI

candidates.label: Building Decision-Making Competence for Humans and AI
candidates.description: Organizations should simultaneously invest in developing human decision-making skills and rigorously measuring AI decision performance.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-Making in the Age of AI

candidates.label: Risk-Based AI Agency Level
candidates.description: The degree of autonomy granted to AI agents should be calibrated according to the risk profile of the decision.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-Making in the Age of AI

candidates.label: Decision Classification Framework
candidates.description: Decisions can be categorized across multiple dimensions including risk, frequency, urgency, horizon, certainty, and the Cynefin domains.
candidates.lesson_title: Decision-Making in the Age of AI
